claim: PIEZO1 and PIEZO2 are newly identified mechanosensitive ion channels that exhibit a preference for calcium in response to mechanical stimuli.
source: PIEZO1 and PIEZO2 are newly identified mechanosensitive ion channels that exhibit a preference for calcium in response to mechanical stimuli.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by citations to prior literature establishing PIEZO1/2 as mechanosensitive channels with calcium preference.

claim: pezo-1 is the sole PIEZO ortholog in Caenorhabditis elegans.
source: In this study, we discovered the vital roles of pezo-1, the sole PIEZO ortholog in Caenorhabditiselegans, in regulating reproduction.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the abstract and introduction, establishing C. elegans has only one PIEZO gene.

claim: Multiple deletion alleles of PEZO-1 caused a severe reduction in brood size.
source: A number of deletion alleles, as well as a putative gain-of-function mutant, of PEZO-1 caused a severe reduction in brood size.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing reduced brood sizes in multiple pezo-1 deletion mutants as shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: A putative gain-of-function mutant of PEZO-1 caused a severe reduction in brood size.
source: A number of deletion alleles, as well as a putative gain-of-function mutant, of PEZO-1 caused a severe reduction in brood size.
evidence: This is supported by data showing the R2405P patient-specific allele reduces brood size (Figure 9C).

claim: Oocytes undergo a variety of transit defects as they enter and exit the spermatheca during ovulation in pezo-1 mutants.
source: In vivo observations showed that oocytes undergo a variety of transit defects as they enter and exit the spermatheca during ovulation.
evidence: This is supported by live imaging data showing oocytes being crushed, pinched, or failing to enter the spermatheca in pezo-1 mutants (Figure 3, Videos 2-5).

claim: Post-ovulation oocytes were frequently damaged during spermathecal contraction in pezo-1 mutants.
source: Post-ovulation oocytes were frequently damaged during spermathecal contraction.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data showing oocytes being crushed as they exit the spermatheca (Figure 3A'-E', Video 3).

claim: Calcium signaling was not dramatically changed in the pezo-1 mutants during ovulation.
source: However, the calcium signaling was not dramatically changed in the pezo-1 mutants during ovulation.
evidence: This is supported by GCaMP3 imaging data showing normal calcium signaling metrics in pezo-1 mutants during early ovulations (Figure 5K-M, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).

claim: Loss of PEZO-1 led to an inability of self-sperm to navigate back to the spermatheca properly after being pushed out during ovulation.
source: Loss of PEZO-1 also led to an inability of self-sperm to navigate back to the spermatheca properly after being pushed out of the spermatheca during ovulation.
evidence: This is supported by sperm distribution assays showing fewer sperm reach the spermatheca in pezo-1 mutants (Figure 7, Figure 8K).

claim: PEZO-1 acts in different reproductive tissues to promote proper ovulation and fertilization in C. elegans.
source: These findings suggest that PEZO-1 acts in different reproductive tissues to promote proper ovulation and fertilization in C. elegans.
evidence: This is supported by tissue-specific degradation experiments showing reduced brood sizes when PEZO-1 is depleted in somatic or germline tissues (Figure 8E-F).

claim: The C. elegans genome encodes 14 mRNA isoforms of pezo-1.
source: The C. elegans genome encodes a single PIEZO ortholog, pezo-1, of which there are 14 mRNA isoformsas the result of differential splicing and transcriptional start sites (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; Harris et al., 2019)
evidence: This is stated explicitly and supported by citation to Harris et al., 2019 and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The 14 mRNA isoforms of pezo-1 code for 12 different PEZO-1 proteins.
source: these 14 isoforms code for 12 different PEZO-1 proteins.
evidence: This is stated explicitly in the Results section.

claim: All pezo-1 isoforms share a common C-terminus.
source: All isoforms share a common C-terminus.
evidence: This is stated explicitly and is relevant for the C-terminal tagging strategy.

claim: GFP::PEZO-1, mScarlet::PEZO-1, and PEZO-1::mScarlet were widely expressed from embryonic stages through adulthood.
source: GFP::PEZO-1, mScarlet::PEZO-1, and PEZO-1::mScarlet were widely expressed from embryonic stages through adulthood (Figure 1B–E,G–J, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–G).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy images showing PEZO-1 expression throughout development.

claim: PEZO-1 is strongly expressed in several tubular tissues, including the pharyngeal-intestinal and spermathecal-uterine valves.
source: Notably, PEZO-1 is strongly expressed in several tubular tissues, including the pharyngeal-intestinal and spermathecal-uterine valves, which is consistent with our hypothesis that pezo-1 may be responsible for mechanoperception in these tissues (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy images and is consistent with the hypothesis about mechanoperception.

claim: PEZO-1 is expressed on the plasma membranes of oocytes and embryonic cells.
source: Under higher magnification, we observed PEZO-1 on the plasma membranes of oocytes and embryonic cells during a variety of embryonic stages, suggesting that PEZO-1 is a transmembrane protein (Figure 1C–E).
evidence: This is supported by high-magnification imaging data showing membrane localization.

claim: PEZO-1 is a transmembrane protein.
source: Under higher magnification, we observed PEZO-1 on the plasma membranes of oocytes and embryonic cells during a variety of embryonic stages, suggesting that PEZO-1 is a transmembrane protein (Figure 1C–E).
evidence: This is inferred from the membrane localization pattern observed in imaging.

claim: PEZO-1 is expressed in multiple reproductive tissues, including the germline, somatic oviduct, and spermatheca.
source: PEZO-1 is expressed in multiple reproductive tissues, including the germline, somatic oviduct, and spermatheca (Figure 1F–J).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy images showing expression in these tissues.

claim: PEZO-1 is expressed on sperm membranes.
source: Higher magnification imaging of the spermatheca revealed that PEZO-1 is also expressed on sperm membranes (Figure 1J).
evidence: This is supported by high-magnification imaging data.

claim: GFP::PEZO-1 is expressed in sheath cells, sperm, both spermathecal valves and the spermathecal bag cells.
source: Live imaging and detailed analysis of PEZO-1 expression patterns during reproduction revealed that GFP::PEZO-1 is expressed in sheath cells, sperm, both spermathecal valves and the spermathecal bag cells (Figure 1K–O, Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by live imaging data during ovulation.

claim: The number of F1 progeny was significantly lower in all tested pezo-1 mutants than in the wild type.
source: However, in all tested pezo-1 mutants, the number of F1 progeny was significantly lower than in the wild type (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by brood size quantification data.

claim: The decrease in brood size was enhanced as pezo-1 mutant animals aged.
source: The decrease in brood size was enhanced as animals aged (36–60 hr post mid-L4, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: This is supported by brood size data at different time points.

claim: The decrease in brood size in pezo-1 mutants was enhanced when grown at a higher temperature (25°C).
source: The decrease in brood size was enhanced as animals aged (36–60 hr post mid-L4, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) or when grown at a higher temperature (25°C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by brood size data at different temperatures.

claim: About 5–25% of F1 embryos failed to hatch from pezo-1 CΔ homozygous mutants.
source: In addition, about 5–25% of F1 embryos failed to hatch from pezo-1 CΔ homozygous mutants (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by embryonic viability data.

claim: Reduced brood sizes were observed when wildtype animals were exposed to 20 μM Yoda1.
source: Reduced brood sizes were observed when wildtype animals were exposed to 20 μM Yoda1 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by brood size data from Yoda1 treatment experiments.

claim: Yoda1 treatment did not worsen the brood size phenotype when pezo-1KO animals were treated.
source: This phenotype did not worsen when pezo-1KO animals were also treated with Yoda (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by brood size data comparing Yoda1 treatment in wildtype and pezo-1 mutants.

claim: Either deletion or overactivation of PEZO-1 is sufficient to disrupt brood size.
source: These data suggest that either deletion or overactivation of PEZO-1 is sufficient to disrupt brood size.
evidence: This is inferred from the Yoda1 treatment data and deletion mutant data.

claim: A large ooplasmic mass was observed in the uteri of pezo-1KO and STOP-IN mutants.
source: Although embryos fill the uterus in wildtype mothers (Figure 2D), a mass of ooplasm in the uteri of both pezo-1KO and STOP-IN mutants was observed (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by DIC microscopy images.

claim: 100% of pezo-1 CΔ and STOP-IN mutant animals had a uterus filled with ooplasm at 60 hr post L4.
source: pezo-1 CΔ and STOP-IN mutants displayed the most severe defects, with 100% of animals having a uterus filled with ooplasm at 60 hr post L4 (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data of uterine ooplasmic masses.

claim: DAPI staining in pezo-1KO uteri revealed chromosome structures indicative of diakinesis-staged oocytes.
source: Staining with DAPI in pezo-1KO uteri revealed chromosome structures that were indicative of diakinesis-staged oocytes (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by DAPI staining images.

claim: Only mitotic chromatin of variably aged embryos were detected in control animals by DAPI staining.
source: By contrast, only mitotic chromatin of variably aged embryos were detected in control animals (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by DAPI staining images of wildtype animals.

claim: BODIPY staining revealed widespread penetration of the entire ooplasmic mass in the uteri of pezo-1 CΔ animals.
source: BODIPY staining revealed widespread penetration of the entire ooplasmic mass in the uteri of pezo-1 CΔ animals (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is supported by BODIPY staining images showing penetration of unfertilized oocytes.

claim: Some oocytes in pezo-1 mutants are not fertilized upon transit through the spermatheca.
source: These data suggest that some oocytes are not fertilized upon transit through the spermatheca and that these unfertilized oocytes may be crushed when they pass through the spermathecal valves.
evidence: This is inferred from DAPI and BODIPY staining data showing unfertilized oocytes in the uterus.

claim: Unfertilized oocytes in pezo-1 mutants may be crushed when they pass through the spermathecal valves.
source: These data suggest that some oocytes are not fertilized upon transit through the spermatheca and that these unfertilized oocytes may be crushed when they pass through the spermathecal valves.
evidence: This is inferred from imaging data showing crushed oocytes and ooplasmic masses.

claim: Reduced numbers of sperm resident in the spermatheca were observed in Day 1 pezo-1 adults.
source: In addition to these apparently crushed oocytes, reduced numbers of sperm resident in the spermatheca were observed in Day 1 pezo-1 adults (0–24 hr post mid-L4) and even fewer were observed in the spermathecae in Day 2–3 adults (24–48 hr post mid-L4) compared with wild type (Figure 2K–M).
evidence: This is supported by sperm counting data using H2B::GFP.

claim: Normal numbers of sperm were present in pezo-1 mutant hermaphrodites prior to the first ovulation.
source: Normal numbers of sperm were present in these mutant hermaphrodites prior to the first ovulation, suggesting that the ability of the sperm to return to the spermatheca after each ovulation was disrupted (Figure 2M).
evidence: This is supported by sperm counting data at different time points.

claim: The ability of sperm to return to the spermatheca after each ovulation was disrupted in pezo-1 mutants.
source: Normal numbers of sperm were present in these mutant hermaphrodites prior to the first ovulation, suggesting that the ability of the sperm to return to the spermatheca after each ovulation was disrupted (Figure 2M).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that sperm numbers decline over time despite normal initial numbers.

claim: Ovulation rates were significantly reduced in pezo-1 CΔ Day 2 animals.
source: Ovulation rates were significantly reduced in pezo-1 CΔ Day 2 (post mid-L4 48 hr) animals (Figure 2N)
evidence: This is supported by ovulation rate quantification data.

claim: The reduction in sperm number could be responsible for the reduction in ovulation rate in pezo-1 mutants.
source: As the presence of sperm in the spermatheca is known to stimulate ovulation (McCarter et al., 1999; Miller, 2001), the reduction in sperm number could be responsible for this reduction in ovulation rate.
evidence: This is inferred based on established knowledge that sperm stimulate ovulation.

claim: The reduced brood size in pezo-1 mutants is probably due to a combination of defects in multiple tissues.
source: Overall, the reduced brood size in pezo-1 mutants is probably due to a combination of defects in multiple tissues, resulting in defective ovulations, crushed oocytes, and defects in the ability of sperm to navigate back into the spermatheca after each ovulation.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on all the observed phenotypes.

claim: In wildtype animals, the contracting sheath cells push the oocyte into the spermatheca, and simultaneously pull the open spermatheca over the oocyte.
source: In wildtype animals, the contracting sheath cells push the oocyte into the spermatheca, and simultaneously pull the open spermatheca over the oocyte (Videos 2 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by live imaging videos of ovulation.

claim: In wildtype animals, once the oocyte enters the spermatheca, both spermatheca valves remain closed during fertilization.
source: Once the oocyte enters the spermatheca, both spermatheca valves remain closed during fertilization (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by live imaging data.

claim: In pezo-1 mutants, many of the oocytes that did successfully enter the spermatheca were crushed when they exited through the sp-ut valve.
source: In pezo-1 mutants, many of the oocytes that did successfully enter the spermatheca were crushed when they exited through the sp-ut valve (Figure 3A′–E′, Videos 2 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by live imaging data showing oocyte crushing.

claim: The sp-ut valve did not completely open when the oocyte attempted to exit the spermatheca in pezo-1 mutants.
source: We observed that the sp-ut valve, labeled by DLG-1::GFP, did not completely open when the oocyte attempted to exit the spermatheca, which may lead to crushing the oocyte (Figure 3C′–E′, Video 3).
evidence: This is supported by live imaging data with DLG-1::GFP marker.

claim: Oocytes in pezo-1 mutants frequently partially entered the spermatheca but were then pinched off and broken into two pieces.
source: During our analysis of the pezo-1 mutants, we frequently observed that oocytes partially entered the spermatheca but were then pinched off and broken into two pieces, one of which remained trapped in the oviduct (proximal gonad; Figure 3F–I, Video 4).
evidence: This is supported by live imaging data showing pinched oocytes.

claim: Some oocytes in pezo-1 mutants failed to enter the spermatheca and slid back into the oviduct.
source: Moreover, some oocytes failed to enter the spermatheca and slid back into the oviduct (Figure 3J–M, Video 5).
evidence: This is supported by live imaging data.

claim: The defective ovulation in pezo-1 mutants is probably due to incomplete constriction of the sheath cells.
source: The defective ovulation is probably due to incomplete constriction of the sheath cells.
evidence: This is inferred from observations of failed oocyte entry.

claim: Feeding itr-1 RNAi resulted in even smaller broods than those observed in pezo-1 mutants alone.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, feeding itr-1 RNAi resulted in even smaller broods than those observed in pezo-1 mutants alone (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by brood size data from RNAi experiments.

claim: Feeding lfe-2 RNAi partially rescued the reduced brood size in pezo-1 mutants.
source: By contrast, feeding lfe-2 RNAi, which should elevate cytosolic Ca2+, partially rescued the reduced brood size (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by brood size data from RNAi experiments.

claim: Depletion of orai-1 led to nearly zero brood size in pezo-1 CΔ mutant but only a 40% reduction in brood size in wild type.
source: Similarly, depletion of the plasma membrane Ca2+ channel orai-1, which is activated to replenish Ca2+in the cytosol from an extracellular source (Lorin-Nebel et al., 2007), led to nearly zero brood size in pezo-1 CΔ mutant but only a 40% reduction in brood size in wild type (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by brood size data from RNAi experiments.

claim: Disruption of ER Ca2+ stores with sca-1 RNAi caused an extremely low brood size in pezo-1 CΔ.
source: Furthermore, disruption of ER Ca2+ stores with sarcoplasmic/ER Ca2+ ATPase (SERCA) sca-1 (RNAi) (Yan et al., 2006) also caused an extremely low brood size in pezo-1 CΔ (Figure 4C)
evidence: This is supported by brood size data from RNAi experiments.

claim: sca-1 RNAi slightly increased the brood size in wild type.
source: whereas sca-1 (RNAi) slightly increased the brood size in wild type (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by brood size data from RNAi experiments.

claim: pezo-1 may function in cytosolic and ER Ca2+ homeostasis, which is crucial for proper spermathecal contractility and dilation.
source: Therefore, these observations are consistent with the hypothesis that pezo-1 may function in cytosolic and ER Ca2+ homeostasis, which is crucial for proper spermathecal contractility and dilation.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic interaction data with calcium regulators.

claim: In wildtype animals, the fluorescent intensity of GCaMP3 at the sp-ut valve immediately increased when the oocyte entered the spermatheca.
source: In wildtype animals, the fluorescent intensity of GCaMP3 at the sp-ut valve immediately increased when the oocyte entered the spermatheca (Figure 5A,F and F', Videos 6 and 7).
evidence: This is supported by GCaMP3 imaging data.

claim: In pezo-1 CΔ mutants, longer transit times of the oocyte through the spermatheca resulted in elongated dwell times.
source: In pezo-1 CΔ mutants, longer transit times of the oocyte through the spermatheca resulted in elongated dwell times (Figure 5K, Video 7)
evidence: This is supported by quantification of dwell time from GCaMP3 imaging.

claim: GCaMP3 fluorescence in pezo-1 mutants was not significantly different from that in the wildtype.
source: Surprisingly, GCaMP3 fluorescence in pezo-1 was not significantly different from that in the wildtype (Figure 5L,M, Video 7; see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is supported by quantification of calcium signaling metrics from GCaMP3 imaging.

claim: Both wildtype and pezo-1 CΔ males are fertile and sire progeny when mated with fem-1(hc17ts) mutants.
source: The fem-1(hc17) animals produced cross-progeny after mating with pezo-1 mutant males, indicating that the pezo-1 mutant males are fertile and that their sperm can crawl through the uterus to the spermatheca upon mating (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by mating assay data.

claim: pezo-1 mutant hermaphrodites resumed ovulation and fertilization upon mating once the male's sperm reached the spermatheca.
source: pezo-1 mutant hermaphrodites resumed ovulation and fertilization upon mating once the male's sperm (from either wildtype or pezo-1 males) reached the spermatheca (Figure 6B–D).
evidence: This is supported by mating assay data showing rescue of ovulation.

claim: The low ovulation rate in older pezo-1 CΔ animals was significantly rescued by spe-9(hc52ts) sperm.
source: Interestingly, the low ovulation rate in older pezo-1 CΔ animals was significantly rescued by spe-9(hc52ts) sperm (Figure 6E), although the ovulated oocytes were not fertilized.
evidence: This is supported by ovulation rate data from mating with spe-9 males.

claim: Purified MSP-fluorescein can trigger ovulation in older pezo-1 C∆ hermaphrodites that are depleted of sperm.
source: An additional experiment was performed to test the ability of the sheath to respond to the sperm signal that triggers ovulation. Even though our data in Figure 6E suggest that just the presence of sperm can trigger ovulation, we went on to show that purified MSP-fluorescein can also trigger ovulation in older pezo-1 C∆ hermaphrodites that are depleted of sperm and are no longer ovulating (Figure 6F–H).
evidence: This is supported by MSP injection experiments.

claim: The absence of self-sperm contributes to a profound reduction of oocyte maturation, ovulation rate, and self-fertility in the aged pezo-1 mutants.
source: Overall, these data suggest that the absence of self-sperm contributes to a profound reduction of oocyte maturation, ovulation rate, and self-fertility in the aged pezo-1 mutants.
evidence: This is inferred from the mating rescue experiments.

claim: In wildtype hermaphrodites, most fluorescent sperm from both wildtype and pezo-1 CΔ males navigated through the uterus and accumulated in the spermatheca.
source: In wildtype hermaphrodites, most fluorescent sperm from both wildtype and pezo-1 CΔ males navigated through the uterus and accumulated in the spermatheca (Figure 7B,C,F,G).
evidence: This is supported by MitoTracker sperm distribution assays.

claim: Fewer fluorescent male sperm reached the spermatheca in Day 3 adult pezo-1 CΔ hermaphrodites.
source: However, fewer fluorescent male sperm reached the spermatheca in Day 3 adult pezo-1 CΔ hermaphrodites, and most sperm remained throughout zones 1 and zone 2, the zones furthest from the spermatheca (Figure 7D,E,H,I).
evidence: This is supported by MitoTracker sperm distribution assays.

claim: In the reproductive tracts of wildtype hermaphrodites, pezo-1 mutant male sperm are motile and display normal navigational behavior.
source: These observations suggest that in the reproductive tracts of wildtype hermaphrodites, pezo-1 mutant male sperm are motile and display normal navigational behavior.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that pezo-1 mutant sperm navigate normally in wildtype hermaphrodites.

claim: In pezo-1 mutant hermaphrodite reproductive tracts, both wildtype and pezo-1 mutant sperm were compromised in their navigational behavior.
source: However, in pezo-1 mutant hermaphrodite reproductive tracts, both wildtype and pezo-1 mutant sperm were compromised in their navigational behavior over the time frame of this experiment.
evidence: This is inferred from the sperm distribution data in pezo-1 hermaphrodites.

claim: In pezo-1 CΔ female mutants, the number of F1 progeny was significantly reduced compared with that in control fem-1(hc17ts) at the permissive temperature of 15°C.
source: In pezo-1 CΔ female mutants, the number of F1 progeny was significantly reduced compared with that in control fem-1(hc17ts) at the permissive temperature of 15°C, which allows for the production of self-sperm (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by brood size data from fem-1 females.

claim: All tested female animals sired crossed progeny but at greatly reduced levels in pezo-1 CΔ females.
source: All tested female animals sired crossed progeny but at greatly reduced levels in pezo-1 CΔ females (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is supported by mating assay data with fem-1 females.

claim: The attractive signal from the oocytes or sheath cells are defective in their ability to attract male sperm to the spermatheca in pezo-1 mutants.
source: This suggests that the attractive signal from the oocytes or sheath cells are defective in their ability to attract male sperm to the spermatheca.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that cross sperm also fail to migrate properly in pezo-1 females.

claim: The defect in the ability to attract sperm to the spermatheca is not just a self-sperm problem.
source: Thus, the defect in the ability to attract sperm to the spermatheca is not just a self-sperm problem; cross sperm from males also fail to migrate to the spermatheca.
evidence: This is inferred from experiments with fem-1 females showing cross sperm also have navigation defects.

claim: The brood sizes were significantly reduced in each of the PEZO-1::Degron strains compared with control.
source: Interestingly, the brood sizes were significantly reduced in each of the PEZO-1::Degron strains compared with control, regardless of the promoter used.
evidence: This is supported by brood size data from auxin-inducible degradation experiments (Figure 8E,F).

claim: The reduction in brood size in PEZO-1::Degron strains was less severe than that observed in the pezo-1ko mutants.
source: However, the reduction in brood size was less severe than that observed in the pezo-1ko mutants (Figures 8E,F and 2A).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of brood size data between degron and knockout strains.

claim: Depletion of PEZO-1 in the somatic tissues led to a variety of ovulation defects.
source: Depletion of PEZO-1 in the somatic tissues, including spermathecal and sheath cells, led to a variety of ovulation defects (Figure 8—figure supplement 3A–I).
evidence: This is supported by live imaging data of somatic-specific degron strains.

claim: Pinched oocytes were frequently observed during ovulation in somatic-specific PEZO-1::Degron animals.
source: Pinched oocytes were frequently observed during ovulation (N = 9/27, Figure 8—figure supplement 3I).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of ovulation defects.

claim: Only 69% of the MitoTracker-labelled wildtype sperm accumulated at the spermatheca in the germline-specific PEZO-1::Degron animals exposed to auxin.
source: Consistent with our male mating experiments, only 69% of the MitoTracker-labelled wildtype sperm accumulated at the spermatheca (zone 3) in the germline-specific PEZO-1::Degron animals exposed to auxin (Figure 8I–K).
evidence: This is supported by sperm distribution data from germline-specific degron strains.

claim: The degradation of PEZO-1 in the germ line interfered with sperm navigation to the spermatheca.
source: Therefore, the degradation of PEZO-1 in the germ line did not cause the severe uterine ooplasmic masses as we have observed for our pezo-1ko mutants but it did interfere with sperm navigation to the spermatheca, suggesting impaired attractant signaling.
evidence: This is inferred from the sperm distribution data in germline-specific degron strains.

claim: Homozygous animals carrying the pezo-1(R2405P) mutation displayed reproductive defects similar to the pezo-1ko mutants.
source: Such homozygotes displayed reproductive defects similar to the pezo-1ko mutants, including reduced ovulation rates, ooplasmic uterine masses (Figure 9B), and reduced brood sizes (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is supported by phenotypic analysis of the R2405P allele.

claim: The phenotypes of pezo-1(R2405P) homozygotes were mildly enhanced in combination with itr-1 RNAi.
source: In addition, the phenotypes of pezo-1(R2405P) homozygotes were mildly enhanced in combination with itr-1 RNAi and suppressed with lfe-2 RNAi, consistent with our findings with pezo-1ko mutants (Figure 9D).
evidence: This is supported by genetic interaction data.

claim: The phenotypes of pezo-1(R2405P) homozygotes were suppressed with lfe-2 RNAi.
source: In addition, the phenotypes of pezo-1(R2405P) homozygotes were mildly enhanced in combination with itr-1 RNAi and suppressed with lfe-2 RNAi, consistent with our findings with pezo-1ko mutants (Figure 9D).
evidence: This is supported by genetic interaction data.

claim: The reduced ovulation rate in pezo-1(R2405P) was significantly rescued by spe-9(hc52ts) sperm.
source: Interestingly, similar to the rescue assay in pezo-1 CΔ, the reduced ovulation rate in pezo-1(R2405P) was also significantly rescued by spe-9(hc52ts) sperm, suggesting that this variant of pezo-1 may similarly disrupt ovulation and sperm-to-sheath signaling, leading to self-sterility (Figure 9E).
evidence: This is supported by mating assay data with the R2405P allele.

claim: C. elegans is an appropriate model system for the study of PIEZO diseases.
source: Overall, these observations support the idea that C. elegans is an appropriate model system for the study of PIEZO diseases.
evidence: This is inferred from the similarity of phenotypes between patient-specific alleles and knockout alleles.

claim: PIEZO1 is a non-selective ion channel that forms homotrimeric complexes at the plasma membrane.
source: PIEZO1 is a non-selective ion channel that forms homotrimeric complexes at the plasma membrane; however, PIEZO1 exhibits a preference for Ca2+ in response to mechanical stimuli (Coste et al., 2010; Gnanasambandam et al., 2015; Syeda et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior literature.

claim: Human and mouse PIEZO1 channels respond to different mechanical stimuli, including static pressure, shear stress and membrane stretch.
source: Recent studies have shown that the human and mouse PIEZO1 channels respond to different mechanical stimuli, including static pressure, shear stress and membrane stretch (Coste et al., 2010; Poole et al., 2014; Ranade et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior literature.

claim: PIEZO1 regulates vascular branching and endothelial cell alignment upon sensing frictional force (shear stress).
source: PIEZO1 also regulates vascular branching and endothelial cell alignment upon sensing frictional force (shear stress) (Li et al., 2015; Nonomura et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior literature.

claim: Stem cells use PIEZO1 to sense mechanical signals and to initiate Ca2+ signaling to promote proliferation and differentiation.
source: Stem cells also use PIEZO1 to sense mechanical signals and to initiate Ca2+ signaling to promote proliferation and differentiation (Del Mármol et al., 2018; He et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior literature.

claim: PIEZO2 primarily functions as a key mechanotransducer for light touch, proprioception and breathing.
source: PIEZO2 primarily functions as a key mechanotransducer for light touch, proprioception and breathing (Nonomura et al., 2017; Woo et al., 2015; Woo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior literature.

claim: Mutations in both human PIEZO1 and human PIEZO2 have been identified among patients suffering from channelopathy diseases.
source: Mutations in both human PIEZO1 and human PIEZO2 have been identified among patients suffering from channelopathy diseases, such as dehydrated hereditary stomatocytosis (DHSt), generalized lymphatic dysplasia (GLD), and distal arthrogryposis type 5 (DA5), in which osmoregulation is disturbed (Albuisson et al., 2013; Andolfo et al., 2013; Bae et al., 2013; Coste et al., 2013; Li et al., 2018; Lukacs et al., 2015; McMillin et al., 2014; Zarychanski et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citations to clinical literature.

claim: Loss-of-function mutations in the PIEZO1 gene cause autosomal recessive congenital lymphatic dysplasia.
source: Loss-of-function mutations in the PIEZO1 gene cause autosomal recessive congenital lymphatic dysplasia, whereas gain-of-function mutations lead to autosomal dominant stomatocytosis (Alper, 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior literature.

claim: Gain-of-function mutations in PIEZO1 lead to autosomal dominant stomatocytosis.
source: Loss-of-function mutations in the PIEZO1 gene cause autosomal recessive congenital lymphatic dysplasia, whereas gain-of-function mutations lead to autosomal dominant stomatocytosis (Alper, 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior literature.

claim: C. elegans hermaphrodites produce sperm during the L4 larval stage and then shift to produce oocytes during the adult stage.
source: C. elegans hermaphrodites produce sperm during the L4 larval stage and then shift to produce oocytes during the adult stage.
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans reproductive biology.

claim: About 150 sperm are stored in each spermatheca of C. elegans hermaphrodites.
source: About 150 sperm are stored in each spermatheca, whereas the oocytes form in the oviduct in each gonad arm.
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans reproductive biology.

claim: Oocyte maturation is triggered by sperm-derived polypeptides known as major sperm proteins (MSPs).
source: Oocyte maturation is triggered by sperm-derived polypeptides known as major sperm proteins (MSPs), which activate the oocyte mitogen-activated protein kinase (MPK-1) (Miller, 2001; Yang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior literature.

claim: MSPs activate the oocyte mitogen-activated protein kinase (MPK-1).
source: Oocyte maturation is triggered by sperm-derived polypeptides known as major sperm proteins (MSPs), which activate the oocyte mitogen-activated protein kinase (MPK-1) (Miller, 2001; Yang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior literature.

claim: The ovulated oocyte spends 3–5 min in the dilated spermatheca with both valves closed to allow the oocyte and sperm to complete fertilization and to initiate eggshell formation.
source: The ovulated oocyte spends 3–5 min in the dilated spermatheca with both valves closed to allow the oocyte and sperm to complete fertilization and to initiate eggshell formation (Johnston et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior literature.

claim: The navigation of the sperm back to the spermatheca is regulated by the chemoattractant prostaglandin, which is secreted by the oocytes and sheath cells.
source: Meanwhile, the sperm that are swept out of the spermatheca during oocyte exit crawl back to the constricted spermatheca. The navigation of the sperm back to the spermatheca is regulated by the chemoattractant prostaglandin, which is secreted by the oocytes and sheath cells (Kubagawa et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior literature.

claim: Supplementing male sperm through mating significantly repopulated the spermatheca with cross-sperm and rescued the extremely low ovulation rate and reduced brood size of pezo-1 mutants.
source: Supplementing male sperm through mating significantly repopulated the spermatheca with cross-sperm and rescued the extremely low ovulation rate and reduced brood size of pezo-1 mutants.
evidence: This is supported by mating rescue experiments (Figure 6B-E).

claim: Reduced brood sizes were observed in each tissue-specific degradation strain of PEZO-1.
source: Reduced brood sizes were observed in each tissue-specific degradation strain, suggesting that PEZO-1 from many tissues has multiple inputs in regulating reproduction.
evidence: This is supported by auxin-inducible degradation experiments (Figure 8E-F).

claim: PEZO-1 from many tissues has multiple inputs in regulating reproduction.
source: Reduced brood sizes were observed in each tissue-specific degradation strain, suggesting that PEZO-1 from many tissues has multiple inputs in regulating reproduction.
evidence: This is inferred from the tissue-specific degradation experiments.

claim: PEZO-1 has a complex role in a number of tissues that are required for reproduction.
source: Thus, our analysis of numerous pezo-1 mutants suggests that PEZO-1 has a complex role in a number of tissues that are required for reproduction.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the experimental data.
